name: interceptor
intent: Let services attach themselves transparently to a framework and be fired automatically when the framework emits named events, so extension code is added, ordered and removed without the framework's core or its clients knowing it exists.
problem: A framework must stay open to services it did not anticipate - logging, metrics, authentication, validation, caching, auditing - and a service must attach transparently to that framework and fire on named events; hard-wiring each concern into the framework's event sites means editing (and retesting and redeploying) code that many other clients depend on, once per concern and per site.
context: Long-lived frameworks and middleware that already define events at stable extension points (request/response phases, RPC calls, device or lifecycle events) and outlive their original requirements; the extension services are cross-cutting, their set and order legitimately change at configuration or run time, and callers must not have to be aware of them. The language must expose some form of late binding - virtual dispatch, function values, annotations, or a dynamic proxy - for attachment to be transparent.
benefits: Services attach and detach without touching the framework's core: no recompilation, no structural change, no awareness on the client side - this transparency is the pattern's defining property.
A single dispatcher becomes the one place where registration, ordering, enablement and scope of all attached services are governed.
The framework gets an evolution path: concerns that were unknown or unwanted when it was designed can be added afterwards, including by third parties.

Cross-cutting services (logging, metrics, tracing, authentication, caching, validation, auditing) are written once and applied uniformly to every relevant event instead of being copied to each call site.
Interceptors interact with the framework only through the event interface and the context object, so they stay independently testable and reusable across framework instances.
Runtime reconfiguration: interceptors can be registered, replaced or removed while the system runs (typically with Component Configurator), which supports staged rollouts and hot fixes.
tradeoffs: Control flow becomes invisible: neither the framework's core code nor its clients see what runs around an event, so a fault can live in the dispatcher, in any registered interceptor, or in the framework itself.

Order is part of the contract - registration order or binding priority silently changes semantics, and most APIs cannot prevent an interceptor from being inserted at a point that invalidates another one.
One interceptor that short-circuits (vetoes, throws, or simply never forwards) disables every downstream interceptor plus the target, so the chain is a shared point of failure for unrelated features.

Registration is state that outlives the component that created it; long-lived frameworks accumulate dead interceptors unless every registration is paired with deterministic deregistration (the listener-leak analogue, which is why ejection APIs exist).
Every event pays for dispatch: a lookup plus context construction per call - negligible next to I/O, but measurable on hot paths and in tight loops.

Interceptors execute on the framework's dispatch thread(s) with the framework's privileges: shared interceptor state needs synchronisation, blocking work stalls the pipeline, and any interceptor sees payloads and internal state the rest of the system assumed were encapsulated.

Emergent behaviour is hard to test and reason about: ordering, short-circuit and multi-interceptor interactions only surface in integration tests, and interception must never be the only enforcement point for a security or correctness rule because a bypass (self-invocation, direct call, unregistered path) defeats it silently.
Because attachment is cheap, the same concern is easily registered twice - double logging, double retries, double charging - with no error raised.

participants.responsibility: Defines the events and owns the points where they are emitted; calls the dispatcher at those points and remains unaware of which concrete services react. New services must be addable without editing it.

Owns the event-to-service mapping and the (de)registration API; for each emitted event it selects the registered interceptors, invokes their callback in the declared order, and implements the chaining/return semantics.
Declares the callback interface a service must implement (the event_callback hook) so the framework can invoke services without knowing their type or purpose.
The added service itself: processes the event, may modify or replace the context, may veto/short-circuit the chain, and (in the POSA2 dynamics) may register or remove further interceptors.
Carries the framework state that is meaningful for this event plus the results accumulated so far; it is the only way an interceptor reads or influences what the framework does next.

use_cases: HTTP middleware: request-id, logging, compression, CORS, body limits and error translation applied to every route without touching handlers (Express, ASP.NET Core, Vapor, Play, Rack, Django, Ktor plugins).
Authentication and authorization gates attached to every call of a framework (gRPC interceptors, Spring HandlerInterceptor, servlet filters, Jakarta Interceptors), producing a uniform 401/403 path.

Observability and audit: metrics, distributed tracing and audit records emitted from framework events instead of scattered call sites; kernel notifier chains serve the same purpose for device, network and error events.
Client-side interception: adding auth headers, retry/backoff, caching or deadlines to outgoing calls (axios interceptors, Angular HTTP interceptors) without changing each caller.

Object-level interception on service interfaces: transactions, caching, lazy loading or authorization woven around method calls by a dynamic proxy or container interceptor (JDK Proxy, DispatchProxy/Castle DynamicProxy, CDI/EJB interceptors).
Runtime reconfiguration of a running system: attaching or removing diagnostic, throttling or feature services in a live framework (POSA2's Interceptor, usually combined with Component Configurator).

Database and ORM interception: attaching audit, soft-delete, or encryption hooks to entity lifecycle events (JPA @PrePersist, Hibernate interceptors, SQLAlchemy event listeners) so persistence concerns stay orthogonal to domain models.

Message broker and event-bus interception: middleware on Kafka consumers, RabbitMQ publishers, or Axon Framework handlers to add tracing headers, schema validation, dead-letter routing, or rate limiting without modifying the business handler.

ORM query interception: wrapping or rewriting repository method calls at the framework level to inject tenant isolation filters, query-level caching, or optimistic-locking retry logic (MyBatis plugin, Django ORM middleware, Spring Data JDBC interceptors).

Express middleware pipelines: app.use() handlers receive req/res/next, may mutate or terminate the request, and must call next() (or next(err)) to continue; loading order therefore makes logging, error handling and route coverage an explicit interceptor-chain concern.

gRPC client and server interceptors apply shared metadata, logging, metrics, caching or policy behavior across unary and streaming RPCs; the configured order determines which interceptor is closer to the network versus the application and therefore what each one observes.

Spring MVC HandlerInterceptor implementations provide preHandle, postHandle and afterCompletion hooks around handlers, but Spring's own guidance directs authentication and authorization to Spring Security's earlier servlet-filter chain because controller-path matching can diverge from interceptor matching.
avoid_when: There is exactly one call site and one concern: a direct call, or the language's own decorator/annotation on that single function, is clearer and cheaper than a dispatcher.

The concern is part of the domain contract and callers must see it: compose explicitly (Decorator, Chain of Responsibility, or a plain higher-order function) so the behaviour appears in the type or call graph.

The extension set and order are fixed at compile time and the language can express them statically: wire policies, template parameters or composed functions and let the compiler check the chain instead of a runtime registry.
The framework already ships a narrower documented extension point for exactly this event - use it rather than layering a second interception mechanism on top.

Interception would be the only enforcement of a security or correctness rule: keep an explicit check on the core path as well, since self-invocation, direct calls or an unregistered route bypass interceptors without any error.
Per-event overhead matters more than extensibility (very hot tight loops, per-packet paths): resolve the chain once, or inline the logic, instead of dispatching per event.
anti_patterns: Business logic living only in interceptors, so the framework becomes an invisible orchestrator that cannot be read from any call site.
Registering interceptors per request, connection or instance and never deregistering them - the listener leak, which is why ejection/clear APIs exist.
Depending on incidental ordering (hash-map iteration, import order, container defaults) instead of declaring and documenting the chain order.
Using interceptors as the only security enforcement point, or leaving a permissive diagnostic interceptor enabled in production where it silently swallows or rewrites events.
Doing blocking I/O or long CPU work inside a dispatch-thread callback and calling it 'cross-cutting'.
A single 'god interceptor' that duplicates the framework's responsibility, so the framework can no longer be used without it.

An interceptor that conditionally skips its own work when a particular header or parameter is present, effectively creating an invisible back-door that lets specific callers bypass cross-cutting enforcement without any error or log entry.

Using a single 'god interceptor' that accumulates auth, logging, metrics, caching and retry logic in one class because the developer wanted one registration point — the framework then becomes unfactorable and impossible to test in isolation.
design_principles: Inversion of control (Hollywood principle): the framework calls the attached service; the service never calls the framework's event sites itself.
Open/closed principle: the framework is open for extension at runtime and closed for modification.
Separation of concerns: cross-cutting services stay out of the framework core, and the core stays out of them.
Single point of control: one dispatcher owns the event-to-service mapping, so registration, ordering and enablement are governable in one place.
Information hiding: the context object exposes exactly the framework state an interceptor is allowed to act on.
best_practices: Define the event set and one narrow extension interface (or callback signature) first, then treat it as a versioned public contract - interceptors break when the events or the context shape change.
Make ordering explicit and documented: provide priority or binding metadata instead of relying on the order in which registrations happened to arrive.
Specify short-circuit and error semantics up front: what a veto does to the remaining chain, whether a throwing interceptor aborts or is isolated, and what the target sees when nothing runs.
Pair every registration with a deterministic deregistration (RAII handle, eject/clear, unregister hook) and test that detaching really removes the interceptor - including during dispatch.
Keep interceptors small, stateless and non-blocking: per-event state belongs in the context, slow work belongs off the dispatch path.
Make the chain observable: record which interceptors ran, in which order and with what verdict, so silent injection, double-registration and accidental vetoes are detectable.
Test the pipeline rather than only the single interceptor: ordering, short-circuit and multi-interceptor interaction are where the defects live.

Define priority bands rather than a flat order: partition the chain into zones (diagnostic → policy → business) so that new interceptors can be placed in the correct zone without requiring every team to coordinate on a single integer. ASP.NET Core's explicit documentation of the recommended middleware order (exception handling → routing → authentication → authorization → business) exemplifies this.

Test the pipeline end-to-end, not just individual interceptors: write integration tests that mount the full dispatcher with all interceptors in a representative configuration and verify that ordering, short-circuit and error-isolation semantics hold. Isolated unit tests of a single interceptor are necessary but not sufficient.

Keep interceptors stateless or ensure thread-safety of shared state: per-call state belongs in the context object; shared mutable state across calls requires synchronisation, which is easy to forget in a multi-threaded server framework and produces subtle correctness bugs that are hard to reproduce.
sources: Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert & Buschmann, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (2000) - Interceptor (Service Access and Configuration chapter; participants, dynamics and consequences).

Microsoft Learn, "ASP.NET Core Middleware" (2026), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/ — covers pipeline ordering, short-circuit, terminal middleware, exception handling, and performance considerations for the canonical .NET HTTP pipeline.

Spring Framework, "Interceptors" (docs.spring.io, 2026), https://docs.spring.io/spring/reference/web/webmvc/mvc-config/interceptors.html — HandlerInterceptor contract (preHandle/postHandle/afterCompletion), MappedInterceptor with include/exclude patterns, and the explicit warning that interceptors are not suited as a security layer.

gRPC Authors, "Interceptors" (grpc.io, 2024), https://grpc.io/docs/guides/interceptors/ — client vs server interceptors, unary vs streaming, chain ordering semantics, and the 'closer to the network / closer to the application' mental model.

Oracle, "Using Interceptors in CDI Applications" (Java EE 7 Tutorial, docs.oracle.com), https://docs.oracle.com/javaee/7/tutorial/cdi-adv006.htm — @AroundInvoke, @Interceptors annotation, beans.xml ordering, @Priority for global ordering, InvocationContext.proceed() semantics.

Expressjs.com, "Writing middleware for use in Express apps" (2026), https://expressjs.com/en/guide/writing-middleware/ — next() contract, middleware loading order, async middleware, error-handling middleware (4-arg signature), and the promise-based auto-forwarding in Express 5.

Ted Neward, "Interceptor Pattern" (Naward Associates blog, 2021), https://blogs.newardassociates.com/patterns/structural/Interceptor/ — interceptor vs Chain of Responsibility (all interceptors run vs first-match aborts), interceptor vs Decorator, and the 'continuation chain' variant.

Express.js, "Using middleware" (official guide, https://expressjs.com/en/guide/using-middleware/) — documents app.use()/router.use() registration, ordered execution, next() continuation, route short-circuiting, and error-handling middleware.

gRPC, "Generated-code reference | Rust" (official documentation, https://grpc.io/docs/languages/rust/generated-code/) — shows configuring interceptors on generated RPC call builders across unary and streaming calls.

Spring Framework, "Interception" (official reference, https://docs.spring.io/spring/reference/web/webmvc/mvc-servlet/handlermapping-interceptor.html) — documents preHandle/postHandle/afterCompletion lifecycle hooks and preHandle short-circuit semantics.

Ben Nadel, "HTTP Interceptors Are An Anti-Pattern That Create Hidden Dependencies And Unnecessary Complexity In Angular" (criticism, https://www.bennadel.com/blog/3589-http-interceptors-are-an-anti-pattern-that-create-hidden-dependencies-and-unnecessary-complexity-in-angular.htm) — critiques global interceptor side effects, hidden dependencies, and debugging complexity.
